short: The Third Succession Act restored both Mary and Elizabeth to the line of succession while maintaining their legal illegitimacy.
full:
Driven by Henry VIII's desire to secure the Tudor dynasty before embarking on a military campaign in France, the Third Succession Act received royal assent in early 1544. It decisively reorganised the succession, reinstating the King's daughters, Mary and Elizabeth, to the line of inheritance behind their younger half-brother, Prince Edward, and his potential heirs.

Crucially, the Act did not legitimise the princesses or validate the marriages of their mothers; they remained legally bastards. It simply named them as statutory heirs, dependent entirely on parliamentary authority and Henry's will. The legislation also reaffirmed the King's right to determine the succession beyond his children, a power he exercised to exclude the descendants of his older sister Margaret in favour of the Suffolk line, setting the stage for future succession disputes.
